questions.prompt: Snellman frames mathematics chiefly as which of the following?
choices: A A closed list of formulas with no modeling role.
B A language for explaining and structuring phenomena.
C Pure memorization of Roman arithmetic.
D A ban on using symbols for quantities.
questions.explain: He presents mathematics as a language, with algebra central to that language.

questions.prompt: Who is typically credited in the lecture with foundational algebra, alongside the Arabic number tradition Snellman praises?
choices: B Only Babylonian scribes with no named book.
questions.explain: Foundational algebra is attributed to Al-Khwarizmi; number system gratitude goes to Arabic mathematicians.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly matches Snellman’s distinction?
choices: A Expression asserts equality; equation never does.
B Equation has an equality; expression does not.
D Neither may contain a variable.
questions.explain: Equation includes “=”; expression is a symbolic form without that assertion.

questions.prompt: A variable, for Snellman, is best described as:
choices: B A symbol standing for an abstract quantity (name is conventional).
C Always the wage amount itself.
questions.explain: Variables are symbols for abstract quantities; labels are arbitrary.

questions.prompt: If you multiply/divide both sides of an inequality by a negative, Snellman requires you to:
choices: A Leave the inequality direction unchanged.
C Convert it into an absolute value.

questions.prompt: A two-variable linear equation in Snellman’s setup looks like:
choices: A ax + cy = d with a, c, d numbers.
questions.explain: Standard form: linear combination of two variables equals a constant.

questions.prompt: Descartes’s contribution emphasized in lecture 2 is:
choices: B Linking algebra to geometry via a coordinate plane.
C Proving all lines have undefined slope.
questions.explain: Cartesian coordinates marry algebra and analytic geometry.

questions.prompt: To find an x-intercept algebraically:
choices: B Set y = 0 and solve for x.

questions.prompt: Slope as “rise over run” means:
choices: A Change in x over change in y only for vertical lines.
B Change in y divided by change in x (rate of tilt).
D Always equal to the y-intercept.

questions.prompt: Slope-intercept form is written:
choices: B y = mx + b, revealing slope m and y-intercept b.
D y − y1 = m(x − x1) exclusively, never y = mx + b.
questions.explain: He highlights y = mx + b for quick graphing.

questions.prompt: For nonzero x, x⁰ equals:
questions.explain: Any nonzero to the 0 power is 1 (0⁰ unsettled).

questions.prompt: Same-base product rule for exponents:
Same-base quotient rule:
choices: C xᵐ / xⁿ = xⁿ⁻ᵐ always only.
D Quotients of powers are illegal.

questions.prompt: x⁻¹ means:
x^(1/2) is identified with:
choices: B The square root of x.

questions.prompt: A function, in Snellman’s machine metaphor:
choices: A May map one valid input to many unrelated outputs freely.
B Takes valid input to an output via a rule.
C Is identical to an inequality.

questions.prompt: Domain means:
choices: B The set of valid inputs.
D Always R excluding nothing for 1/x.

questions.prompt: For 1/x, exclude from the domain:
Range of x ↦ x² over the reals:
Composition of functions is:
choices: A Ordinary addition of outputs only.
B Feeding one function’s output into another function.
D The same as dividing domains.
questions.explain: Composition is the new operation beyond ±×÷.

questions.prompt: Degree of a polynomial is:
choices: B Highest power with nonzero coefficient.
D The constant term’s absolute value.

questions.prompt: Degree 2 polynomials are called:
If the leading coefficient of an apparent quadratic is 0:
choices: B Degree drops (no longer genuinely degree 2).
questions.explain: Leading coefficient must be nonzero to keep the claimed degree.

questions.prompt: Multiplying polynomials fundamentally uses:
choices: A Only cancellation of unlike terms.

questions.prompt: Polynomial long division is presented as:
choices: B An abstraction of numeric quotient/remainder long division.
questions.explain: Same long-division principles lifted to polynomials.

questions.prompt: Why is “√1 = ±1” the wrong reading of the square-root function?
choices: A Because functions must give a single output; √1 = 1.
B Because 1 has no square root.
C Because negative numbers square to negatives.
D Because square roots are undefined at 1.
questions.explain: Single-valued square-root function vs. two algebraic solutions of x² = 1.

questions.prompt: Factoring x² − 1 aims at writing it as:
choices: A A sum of cubes only.
B A product of linear factors set to zero.

questions.prompt: Before completing the square, Snellman wants:
choices: A Leading coefficient 1 (factor out if needed).
C b removed permanently without adjusting.

questions.prompt: The quadratic formula solves:
choices: B ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
C Systems of five lines only.
D Domain questions for logs exclusively.

questions.prompt: Snellman’s take on “imaginary” numbers includes:
choices: A They are useless historically and now.
B The name is historical; such quantities appear in real applications (e.g., flight).
C They contradict the quadratic formula.
questions.explain: He defends their reality via applications despite the name.

questions.prompt: Doubling grains of rice square-by-square illustrates:
choices: D A system with no solution.

questions.prompt: Allowed bases b for bˣ in his discussion exclude:
choices: B b = 0 and b = 1 (and he uses 0<b<1 or b>1).

questions.prompt: log_b is introduced as:
choices: B The inverse function of bˣ.
D A type of cubic polynomial.

questions.prompt: A key use of logarithms in solving equations is:
choices: B Bringing exponents down to apply algebra.
questions.explain: Same-base log pulls the exponent out.

questions.prompt: Domain of log_b is:
A solution of a linear system must:
choices: A Satisfy one equation chosen at random.
C Be the slope of each line.
D Be undefined if there are two variables.

questions.prompt: Two distinct parallel lines as a system yield:
questions.explain: Parallel distinct lines never meet → no solution.

questions.prompt: Unlike many quadratics, linear systems do not allow:
choices: B Exactly two solutions (as a separate case).
questions.explain: Trichotomy only: unique / none / infinitely many.

questions.prompt: Elimination is highlighted because:
choices: A Substitution always scales better to huge systems.
B It systematically removes variables and leads toward matrices/linear algebra.
C It requires completing the square.
D It only works for parallel lines.
questions.explain: Elimination + matrices as the powerful method.

questions.prompt: Snellman motivates systems partly by noting:
choices: A GPS technology uses this mathematics.
C Systems are unrelated to fitting curves.
D Only pure number theory uses them.
questions.explain: He cites phone GPS as a concrete relevance hook.
